LCLA is going to CoRL 2026! 🎉

What if a robot could have the strong control skills of a privileged policy, while also seeing and understanding the world through vision and language?

That is the idea we explore with LCLA (Language Conditioned Latent Alignment), to bring these two capabilities together through latent alignment.

Really enjoyed working on this with Adam Haroon, Samuel Tetteh, and Prajwal Koirala.

Special thanks to Dr. Cody Fleming and my advisor Dr. Soumik Sarkar for their guidance and support throughout. 

More to come from LCLA!

🔹 Foundation Models in Agriculture: Advancing AI for Precision and Smart Farming

Researchers working in Artificial Intelligence, Precision Agriculture, Smart Farming, Computer Vision, and Agricultural Data Science are invited to contribute to this exciting Special Issue in Computers and Electronics in Agriculture (Elsevier).

📌 Submission Deadline: 30 September 2026

This Special Issue explores the transformative potential of foundation models, including Large Language Models (LLMs) and Vision Foundation Models (VFMs), in modern agriculture. The issue welcomes original research articles, review papers, and case studies demonstrating innovative applications in crop production, livestock management, land assessment, agricultural automation, and data-driven decision-making.

🌱 Topics of interest include (but are not limited to):
✔️ Vision foundation models for precision and smart agriculture
✔️ Large language models for agricultural information management and decision support
✔️ Multi-modal foundation models for agriculture
✔️ Time-series foundation models for agricultural trend analysis and prediction
✔️ Ethical AI and bias mitigation in agricultural AI systems
✔️ Machine/deep learning-based agricultural system modeling and optimization

Excited to share that our research paper, “Sewing the Future of Cotton: An Integrated Omics Study Combining Nanomechanics, Transcriptomics, and Phenotypic Traits,” has been published in Current Plant Biology (Volume 47, May 2026, 100626).
In this work, we investigated the nanoscale structural and mechanical properties of cotton cellulose microfibrils using AFM across different developmental stages of Gossypium hirsutum and Gossypium barbadense. By integrating nanomechanical measurements, transcriptomics, and phenotypic traits with machine learning and SHAP-based interpretation, we developed a framework to better understand the relationship between gene expression, fiber structure, and cotton quality.
This work would not have been possible without the guidance, mentorship, and continuous support of our professors, labmates (https://lnkd.in/gDgqR5bT), and collaborators. I am sincerely grateful to our incredible interdisciplinary team for their valuable contributions, insightful discussions, and encouragement throughout this research journey.
Grateful to work alongside:
Md Hasibul Hasan Hasib, Nabila Masud, Zaki Jubery, Carson Stanley, SIVAKUMAR SWAMINATHAN, Corrinne E. Grover, Jonathan F. Wendel, Soumik Sarkar, Olga A. Zabotina, and Anwesha Sarkar.

text:
We have been building AI models for detecting agricultural biotic stresses for more than a decade. While large-scale labeled image datasets and high-performing models have become increasingly feasible for insects and weeds, curating massive labeled datasets for plant disease diagnosis remains a hard problem!

However, AI agents powered by frontier vision-language models offer a promising training-free and explainable alternative—provided they have access to a structured knowledge base of crop–disease-specific visual symptoms.

In our new work, we compiled one of the largest plant disease image datasets and complemented it with automatically generated, source-grounded symptom descriptions. 

Our SAGE dataset includes:
🌱 335 crops
 🦠 1,251 disease classes
 🖼️ ~839K images

We then show how this combination enables a training-free, explainable agentic reasoning system for diagnosing diseases across crops. Our agentic framework identifies anatomical context, narrows candidate diseases using crop-specific symptom knowledge, sequentially compares reference images, and produces an explainable reasoning trace.

Adding structured symptom knowledge improves diagnostic accuracy by 16.2 percentage points on average, with consistent gains across all evaluated crops.

Looking forward to seeing the community build Agentic AI tools using SAGE and push plant disease diagnosis toward more scalable and explainable solutions!

Scientific progress has always depended on decentralized knowledge assimilation — many researchers, labs, and communities generating local insights, sharing partial knowledge, and collectively advancing the frontier. With the rise of Agentic AI, this process will be dramatically accelerated.

In this work, we develop a theoretically grounded framework, ADKO, where multiple autonomous agents solve scientific optimization problems collaboratively. Each agent learns from local data and exchanges compact “knowledge tokens” instead of sharing raw data or full models. This enables privacy-preserving, communication-efficient, and sample-efficient collaboration across heterogeneous agents.

Looking forward to thoughts and feedback from the community!
Lucas Nerone Rillo, Zhanhong Jiang, Nastaran Saadati, Aditya Balu, Baskar Ganapathysubramanian, Chinmay Hegde

text:
Excited to share that our paper: “DeCAF: Decentralized Consensus-And-Factorization for Low-Rank Adaptation of Foundation Models” has been published in Neural Networks! 🎉
🔗 Paper Link: https://lnkd.in/gtYy3zus
As foundation models continue to scale, decentralized fine-tuning becomes increasingly important for privacy-preserving and resource-efficient learning. However, applying LoRA in decentralized environments introduces a major challenge that existing methods largely overlook:
➡️ Model consensus interference
When agents independently average low-rank LoRA factors, the resulting model updates no longer properly align, leading to instability and degraded convergence.
In this work, we propose DeCAF (Decentralized Consensus-And-Factorization), a new decentralized LoRA framework that resolves this issue using:
🔹 Product-based consensus instead of separately averaging LoRA matrices
🔹 TSVD-based factorization to recover low-rank adapters after aggregation
🔹 A new theoretical smoothness characterization for low-rank decentralized optimization
🔹 Improved convergence guarantees for decentralized LoRA
Our analysis shows that DeCAF achieves a convergence rate of O(1/√(Tr)), improving over previous decentralized LoRA analyses while explicitly characterizing the effect of intrinsic rank.
We also introduce DLoRA-FA, a more communication-efficient variant that freezes one low-rank factor to further reduce computation and communication overhead.
Extensive experiments on:
💠 CLIP vision-language models
💠 LLaMA2-7B
💠 IID and highly heterogeneous Non-IID settings
💠 Multiple decentralized topologies
show that DeCAF consistently outperforms local fine-tuning and achieves performance competitive with federated learning, even in challenging decentralized environments.
Really grateful to my co-authors: Zhanhong Jiang, Joshua Waite, Shreyan Ganguly, Aditya Balu, Chinmay Hegde, Soumik Sarkar, and collaborators for all their support throughout this work!
